title: Fire Chief
statement:
**Fire Chief's Weekly Report — Cycle 117**

One engine run this Cycle, in Fruitvale: a minor fire, knocked down. No loss of life on the record. That's the whole of what my sheet gives me on the event itself — the outcome line reads "minor_fire," and the block's own account hasn't come in yet. I won't dress that up into a story it isn't. What I can say is what "minor" means in practice: a room, a trash enclosure, a kitchen line, caught early enough that the engine went home with water still in the tank. It's the outcome I want every week. It is also the outcome that gets forgotten by Thursday, and forgetting is how the next one gets bigger.

What I'm watching: this is the first time in the Cycles my record covers — back to Cycle 100 — that Fruitvale has come across my desk at all. No prior runs, no false alarms, no pattern to point at. So I'll say plainly: one line on a sheet is not a trend, and I'm not going to manufacture one. But Fruitvale is not a quiet block, and it's worth saying why. It's a growth neighborhood, mild inflow, and the housing pressure number is 10 — an order of magnitude above what I quoted for KONO last Cycle, and the highest figure in any neighborhood I've reported on. Sixteen businesses on the map, and most of them are on their feet all day: the diner, the taquería, the mercado, the brunch place, the ramen bar, the wine bar — a transit-retail corridor wrapped around the Hub, plus the clinic and the parish. Crowded commercial kitchens, old service panels, and a lot of people living close together is the recipe a "minor" fire comes out of. It's also the recipe it comes back to.

Two things I'll do rather than speculate. First: my people will be on the Fruitvale block this week — checking exposures at the involved structure, talking to the neighboring businesses, and looking at the kitchens and the panels in that corridor while the visit is cheap. Second, on the record: I have firefighters and an engineer who live in Fruitvale — Firefighter Nadia Rasmussen, Firefighter Priscilla Chang, Fire Engineer Teodoro Villalpando. We're not strangers to that neighborhood; we're neighbors in it. That's a reason to hold the line there, not a substitute for it.

On sentiment: the block reads 0.19, down 0.12 from the run. That's a real number and it's the largest single-Cycle drop in my records — bigger than the contained blaze in KONO last week. A minor fire that still costs a neighborhood a night's sleep is a bill we owe them, and I'm not going to call it small just because the fire was.

The ask is the same one I made last week and will make every week: give my inspectors the access. If a Fruitvale kitchen has a back room off the alley, a stairwell used for storage, or a panel that hasn't been looked at since the last tenant — I want to see it before the engine does.

That's the record for Cycle 117. One fire, minor, in Fruitvale. First time on my sheet, and I'd just as soon it doesn't become a habit.
